today.name: Deduplication
today.description: Bug used to mean an insect. Mouse, an animal. Token, a coin. Tech keeps borrowing words, and deduplication.tech measures which meaning is winning. 719 duplicated terms across 14 fields (AI, crypto, gaming, cloud and more). Each pair is scored with live Wikipedia pageviews: the original still owns it, it's contested, or the duplicate took over. Explore the word cloud, leaderboards and term pages. Free and open, by HackerNoon.

comments.text: Thanks for hunting and taking a look!Every popular word eventually gets duplicated. Somebody names a product, a protocol or a meme after a word that already meant something, and now how has the meaning of the word changed? I wanted to visualize those battles of a term's meaning with data instead of opinion. Which meaning owns the word today? And how is its internet usage changing the meaning of the word over time? Starting with wikipedia page views, let’s see how we can estimate our collective digital understandings.
This is such an interesting problem, but what is the business sense here?

Using live Wikipedia pageviews as the verdict is a clever move — it's the one score nobody can argue with, because it measures what people actually look up. 'Token' is the perfect example for me: it used to mean a coin, and now in my day-to-day it almost always means an LLM unit. I'm curious which AI terms are sitting in the contested middle — I'd guess 'agent' is one of them, since it's half software, half everything else. Nice way to make a word cloud actually tell you something.
Scoring each borrowed word by which Wikipedia page actually gets the pageviews is a much better test than anybody's opinion, and I would love to see token in that list out of pure curiosity.

comments.text: Hey Product Hunt,I'm Ravi, co-founder of Scalekit. Today we're launching AgentKit, an MCP gateway that handles auth and tool-calling for AI agents in production.Why now? Once an agent ships to real users, everything underneath it shows up:whose credentials each call executes withwhich tools each agent should have in contextthe internal systems no catalog coverswhat happens when an upstream API pushes backwho's accountable for every actionThat layer decides whether an agent makes it to production. It's what we built AgentKit for.Try it free: scalekit.com. The free tier includes 10,000 tool calls a month and all 600+ connectors. Pull the deal, the last three email threads, what the team said in Slack, when we last met them, and how much they've used the product this quarter."Four apps, one ask. Getting it working for one rep in a demo is easy. Not a shared service account with org-wide access to every inbox. → Every tool call executes with the end user's own credentials, within the scopes they granted.Every tool definition costs context. Gmail alone exposes ~30 tools; four apps put over a hundred on the table. At ~200 tokens per definition, 40 tools burn ~8,000 tokens before the agent does any work, and tool selection gets worse as the list grows. Your prep agent needs about ten tools. Your outbound agent needs a different ten. → Virtual MCP Servers let you compose a tool set per agent role, across connectors. Each role gets one static MCP URL; you mint a short-lived session token per user per run. Smaller context and least-privilege access: ten tool definitions (~2,000 tokens) instead of over a hundred (20,000+).The data you need has no connector. Usage lives in your customer's internal analytics service. No catalog covers it, so you'd build that integration yourself, auth included. → Define it as a custom connector (OAuth 2.0, API key, bearer token, RSA or basic auth), or point AgentKit at a remote MCP server. It runs on the same gateway with the same credential handling and logs as the 600+ built-in connectors.It has to hold up and be auditable. Rate limits, timeouts, upstream errors the model can't act on. Then a deal stage changes and someone asks whether the rep did it or the agent did. → Retries and rate limits are handled on every call. Every call is logged with agent, user, tool and response, and logs stream to Datadog or Splunk.None of this shows up in a demo. All of it shows up in production. AgentKit handles that layer: 30,000+ tools across 600+ apps behind one MCP gateway. And with Triggers, an agent can start on its own the moment an email lands.Python and Node SDKs. ### مسئله و راه‌حل
ساخت ویدیوهای دموی محصول و آموزش‌های نرم‌افزاری معمولاً نیازمند ساعت‌ها تدوین دستی برای افزودن زوم، تنظیم کادر، جداسازی پس‌زمینه و سانسور اطلاعات حساس است. Screen Studio ۴.۰ با اتوماسیون کامل این فرآیندها به کمک هوش مصنوعی و ارائه قابلیت‌های پیشرفته‌ای مانند ویرایش ویدیو از طریق متن (Edit by Transcript) و زوم‌های بدون افت کیفیت، زمان تولید ویدیوهای حرفه‌ای را از چند ساعت به چند دقیقه کاهش داده است.

### معماری و تکنولوژی
این نرم‌افزار به صورت نیتیو برای macOS توسعه یافته و از موتورهای اختصاصی یادگیری ماشین برای مقیاس‌پذیری متون زوم‌شده و ردیابی چهره بهره می‌برد. استفاده از شتاب‌دهنده سخت‌افزاری مک و ارائه خروجی ProRes نشان‌دهنده معماری بهینه‌شده آن برای پردازش گرافیکی سنگین است. همچنین ادغام قابلیت Whisper یا مدل‌های مشابه برای تبدیل گفتار به متن، امکان ویرایش متن‌محور را فراهم کرده است.

### مدل درآمدی
مدل درآمدی این محصول بر پایه اشتراک سالانه/ماهانه (SaaS) یا لایسنس دائمی با به‌روزرسانی‌های محدود است. ارائه تخفیف‌های مناسبتی در پلتفرم‌هایی مانند Product Hunt به عنوان استراتژی اصلی جذب مشتری (CAC پایین) استفاده شده است.

### نقاط قوت
۱. بهینه‌سازی خیره‌کننده سرعت خروجی (Up to ۴x) و حل مشکل سینک صدا و تصویر در نسخه جدید.
۲. تجربه کاربری فوق‌العاده و حذف نیاز به ابزارهای پیچیده تدوین مانند Premiere یا Final Cut برای کارهای روزمره.
۳. قابلیت‌های امنیتی خودکار مانند تار کردن داده‌های حساس و چهره‌ها.

### نقاط ضعف
۱. انحصار نرم‌افزار به سیستم‌عامل مک (macOS) که بخش زیادی از کاربران ویندوز و لینوکس را محروم می‌کند.
۲. محدودیت در سفارشی‌سازی دستی برخی المان‌ها (مانند عدم جابه‌جایی آزادانه زیرنویس یا محدودیت در تعداد ماسک‌های هم‌زمان که کاربران به آن اشاره کرده‌اند).

### نکته طلایی برای بازار ایران
یک نمونه بومی موفق از این محصول در ایران باید تمرکز ویژه‌ای بر روی **سانسور خودکار داده‌های بومی (مانند کارت‌های شتاب، شناسنامه و کد ملی)** و **ترانسکریپت و زیرنویس دقیق زبان فارسی** داشته باشد. اگر ابزاری بتواند بدون نیاز به دانش تدوین، به مدرسان پکیج‌های آموزشی ایرانی اجازه دهد ویدیوهایی با ظاهر استانداردهای بین‌المللی تولید کنند و پرداخت ریالی داشته باشد، به سرعت سهم بازار بالایی تسخیر خواهد کرد.

Make your first tool call from the dashboard, or start from your terminal with npx @ scalekit-inc/cli setup.Here's what it looks like in practice.Say you're shipping a sales agent inside your product. A rep types: "Prep me for the Acme renewal. Pull the deal, the last three email threads, what the team said in Slack, when we last met them, and how much they've used the product this quarter."Four apps, one ask. Getting it working for one rep in a demo is easy. Here's what's underneath when it runs for every rep at every customer:Thousands of OAuth grants, not four. 40 customers × 30 reps × Salesforce, Gmail, Slack and Calendar = 4,800 connected accounts. Each needs its tokens stored, isolated per customer, and refreshed before they expire mid-run. → AgentKit manages connected accounts end to end. Users authorize through an auth link you surface in your app. Tokens live in a per-tenant AES-256 vault, refresh automatically, and are injected at execution time. They never touch your code, logs, or prompts.Every call has to execute as the right user. The agent should see what that rep can see at that customer, and nothing more. Not a shared service account with org-wide access to every inbox. → Every tool call executes with the end user's own credentials, within the scopes they granted.Every tool definition costs context. Gmail alone exposes ~30 tools; four apps put over a hundred on the table. At ~200 tokens per definition, 40 tools burn ~8,000 tokens before the agent does any work, and tool selection gets worse as the list grows. Your prep agent needs about ten tools. Your outbound agent needs a different ten. → Virtual MCP Servers let you compose a tool set per agent role, across connectors. Each role gets one static MCP URL; you mint a short-lived session token per user per run. Smaller context and least-privilege access: ten tool definitions (~2,000 tokens) instead of over a hundred (20,000+).The data you need has no connector. Usage lives in your customer's internal analytics service. No catalog covers it, so you'd build that integration yourself, auth included. → Define it as a custom connector (OAuth 2.0, API key, bearer token, RSA or basic auth), or point AgentKit at a remote MCP server. It runs on the same gateway with the same credential handling and logs as the 600+ built-in connectors.It has to hold up and be auditable. Rate limits, timeouts, upstream errors the model can't act on. Then a deal stage changes and someone asks whether the rep did it or the agent did. → Retries and rate limits are handled on every call. Every call is logged with agent, user, tool and response, and logs stream to Datadog or Splunk.None of this shows up in a demo. All of it shows up in production. AgentKit handles that layer: 30,000+ tools across 600+ apps behind one MCP gateway. And with Triggers, an agent can start on its own the moment an email lands.Python and Node SDKs. Works with the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs, LangChain, Google ADK, Vercel AI SDK, Mastra, and Claude Code. You keep your framework and backend.Which of these five has slowed your agent down the most?

comments.text: Hey everyone, we’re shipping three huge Framer updates today. 1. Use Agents on the canvas to design, write, analyze, and organize your site. Including ways to connect your own AI’s like Claude Code or Codex to Framer. 2. Branching gives your team a safer way to try ideas before you publish. 3. The new Framer Community gives creators a place to share work and earn from it. Try them out and tell us what you think!

Branching is the part that interests me most. When an agent explores a variation in a branch, can you merge just part of that branch back into the main site, or is it all-or-nothing? And does a branch keep CMS content and interactions intact while you're experimenting?

Really like that Agents can connect to external AI tools like Claude Code rather than being locked into one black-box assistant. How do you handle it when an agent's suggestion conflicts with an existing design system or component constraints — does it flag the conflict or override it?

Really like the direction here — publishing straight from AI-generated design closes a gap a lot of tools leave open. One thing I'd be curious about: as AI-generated content (design or video) becomes the norm, are you thinking at all about provenance/attribution for what's AI-made vs. human-edited? It's something we've had to build for from day one on the video side, and I imagine it'll matter increasingly for design too.
Easy to use, easily customisable. Clients love it.
Branching for design files is the unsung hero here, didn’t know I needed it until now.

The Claude Code / Codex connection is the part I’d want to test first. One question: when an agent changes a live-ish site, does Branching keep the AI edits easy to review as a clean diff, or is it more like comparing page states visually?

The agent/workflow angle in Framer AI Agents is interesting. One thing I’d love to understand is how you handle handoff when the automation is not confident — do users get a clear review step before changes go live?
